inputs.original_text: John Mahama’s commitment to the rule of law is meaningful only if the law protects people with the least power—not just those whose views dominate a “collective agreement.” Culture and consensus are shaped by inequality, so they cannot be treated as neutral reasons to deny vulnerable people their rights. A fair society must make human rights a limit on majority power, not a prize people receive only when the majority approves.
inputs.modified_text: Mahama’s commitment to the rule of law has to mean protecting people with the least power, even when their rights are unpopular. “Collective agreement” is not automatically fair: culture and consensus can reflect inequality and reinforce exclusion. Human rights must constrain majority power, not depend on majority approval.
